common_name: Karenbana Azalea (Pink-and-Purplish-Red Satsuki Hybrid of Karenko)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Karenbana was registered in Japan in 2004 from a cross of Koyo and Karenko and carries the Karenko sport line forward into a new named hybrid.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to protect the shallow root system from heat and drought stress. Karenbana resulted from crossing the seedling cultivar Koyo with Karenko pollen, combining genes from the influential Juko-Karenko breeding line, and bears medium-sized flowers with a pink ground overlaid by purplish-red secondary markings. Its name, often translated along the lines of a romantic or showy blossom, reflects the layered bicolor effect of the bloom rather than any fragrance trait. As with other Satsuki selections, it flowers later in the season than Kurume or Southern Indica azaleas and sets next year's buds soon after that late bloom, so prune only immediately after flowering finishes.
sources: Azalea Variety Database (azaleadatabase.com) — Karenbana cultivar page
Azalea Society of America — The Azalean, Development of New Satsuki Azalea Hybrids

common_name: Masazuki Azalea (White-and-Pink Satsuki Hybrid of Karenko)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Masazuki was registered in Japan in 2003 using Karenko as the seed parent, making it one of several Karenko-line hybrids grown mainly by Satsuki collectors.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root zone cool and evenly moist. Masazuki carries Karenko as its seed parent crossed with the cultivar Mibu-no-Hana, producing medium-sized flowers with a white base lightly washed in pink rather than the bolder bicolor pattern of Karenko itself. Like its parent and siblings in the Juko-Karenko line, it blooms later in the season than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, typically in late spring to early summer. Its modest, compact stature and small dark leaves make it well suited to container culture and bonsai training as much as general border planting.
sources: Azalea Variety Database (azaleadatabase.com) — Masazuki cultivar page
Azalea Society of America — The Azalean, Development of New Satsuki Azalea Hybrids

common_name: Aiko Azalea (Small Lavender-and-Purple Satsuki Hybrid of Karenko)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Aiko was registered in Japan in 2002 from a cross of Hakurin and Karenko and is grown mainly among Satsuki collectors and bonsai enthusiasts.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to protect the shallow root system from drought and heat. Aiko was bred from the white cultivar Hakurin crossed with Karenko pollen, and it carries small flowers with a lavender ground overlaid by purple secondary markings, a cooler-toned departure from the warmer pink and white tones of other Karenko-line hybrids. It flowers later in the season than most Kurume and Southern Indica azaleas, in keeping with its Satsuki heritage, and its small leaves and compact habit make it a popular subject for bonsai training as well as container growing. Prune only right after flowering, since next year's buds set soon afterward.
sources: Azalea Variety Database (azaleadatabase.com) — Aiko cultivar page
Azalea Society of America — The Azalean, Development of New Satsuki Azalea Hybrids

common_name: Byakuren Azalea (White-Based Sport of Karenko Satsuki Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Byakuren arose as a white-flowered sport of Karenko, itself a two-color sport of Juko, and has since been used as a breeding parent in its own right.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, mulching to keep the shallow root system evenly moist. Byakuren is a sport of Karenko that lost its parent's pink-and-bicolor pigment in favor of a white flower base, a mutation similar in nature to the way Karenko itself arose as a color sport of Juko. Japanese breeders have since used Byakuren as a parent crossed with the red cultivar Koyo to raise further named Satsuki hybrids with pastel, patterned blooms. Like other plants in the Juko-Karenko lineage it flowers later in the season than Kurume or Southern Indica azaleas and should be pruned only immediately after bloom, since next year's flower buds form soon afterward.
sources: Azalea Variety Database (azaleadatabase.com) — Development of New Satsuki Azalea Hybrids in Japan
Azalea Society of America — The Azalean, Development of New Satsuki Azalea Hybrids

common_name: Clarise Carleton Camellia (Large Semi-Double Pinkish-Red Japonica, Parent of Royalty)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade sheltered from wind and early morning sun; Clarise Carleton was registered in the United States in the mid-1950s and later became one of the two parents of the hybrid cultivar Royalty.

directions: Clarise Carleton is a vigorous, upright Camellia japonica with very large, glossy, dark green leathery leaves and loose, semi-double, pinkish-red flowers that open from midwinter into early spring. It is sometimes seen misspelled in nursery and gardening sources as 'Clarise Carlton', though the name as registered in the United States in the mid-1950s uses the 'Carleton' spelling. The cultivar is best known today as one of the two parents, alongside the reticulata selection Chang's Temple, behind the widely grown hybrid Royalty, and it remains a worthwhile garden plant in its own right for its heavy flowering and handsome foliage. Site it in acidic, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil in a sheltered spot with partial to full shade, protecting buds and open flowers from harsh wind and direct early morning sun after a freeze.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Camellia japonica 'Clarise Carleton'

common_name: Insignis Orange Angel's Trumpet (Parent of Inca Sun)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after frost danger has passed in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this warm-group selection has been grown in the trade since Logee's first listed it in 1990 and was later used as the pod parent of the hybrid 'Inca Sun'.

directions: 'Insignis Orange' bears single, nodding, funnel-shaped flowers in warm yellow-orange tones typical of the warm-group Brugmansia hybrids sold alongside it as 'Insignis Gold', 'Insignis Coral', 'Insignis Pink', and similar named selections. Despite its name, growers and registries note that the plant grown in cultivation under this name is not a true cultivar of the species Brugmansia insignis, and the nomenclature has long been disputed; material sold as 'Insignis Orange' has in some cases been renamed 'USA Orange' to resolve the confusion, though 'Insignis Orange' remains the name under which it is most widely grown and sold. It is best known today as the pod parent, crossed with 'Betty Marshall' as the pollen parent, behind the hybrid 'Inca Sun', bred by Kyle Courtney and introduced through the Gottschalk retail list in 2003. Like other warm-group Brugmansia, it has no frost tolerance and should be cut back and heavily mulched or moved under cover before freezing weather; all parts of the plant are highly toxic if ingested.
sources: Brugmansia Growers International cultivar registry — Insignis Orange and Inca Sun
